title: Authentic Carbonara
kicker: Guanciale, egg, pecorino, pepper. No cream. We need to talk about the no cream thing.
story: Carbonara is a dish with exactly four ingredients and a thousand opinions. Romans make it with guanciale — cured pork jowl, richer and silkier than bacon — pecorino romano, eggs, and a scandalous amount of black pepper. Cream is not in the recipe anywhere, and adding it is the fastest way to make an Italian grandmother sigh audibly in your general direction.

The technique lives in a narrow band of temperature. You want the eggs to turn into a custard that coats the pasta — glossy, flowing, tender. One degree too hot and you get scrambled eggs with spaghetti. The insurance policy is simple: work off the heat, use plenty of cheese in the egg mixture, and loosen with pasta water until the sauce pours like heavy cream.
fun_fact: Carbonara's first written appearance is only from 1950, and American cream shows up in early versions. The 'authenticity wars' are younger than most people's grandparents.

ingredients.note: pork jowl; pancetta is the substitute, bacon the last resort
the biggest, freshest eggs you can find
finely grated, plus more at the table
toast it in the pork fat
lighter than usual — guanciale and pecorino are salty

steps.title: Render the guanciale
steps.text: Cut into thick matchsticks. Start in a cold pan over medium-low and let the fat render slowly for 8-10 minutes until deep gold and glassy. Kill the heat and leave the fat in the pan — this is your sauce base.

steps.title: Whisk the eggs and cheese
steps.text: Yolks, whole egg, pecorino, half the pepper. It forms a thick paste — loosen with a spoonful of pasta water until it looks like wet sand turning to cream.

steps.title: Toast the pepper, cook the pasta
steps.text: Salted water, rigatoni or spaghetti a minute under al dente. While it boils, warm the black pepper in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant — small move, big aroma.

steps.title: The custard maneuver
steps.text: Pull pasta directly into the pan with a splash of its water. Toss. Then, OFF the heat, add the egg mixture and toss like your dinner depends on it — it does. Add pasta water in splashes until the sauce turns glossy and coats a spoon.

steps.title: Serve before it sets
steps.text: Warm bowls. Top with the crisp guanciale, remaining pepper, and a snowfall of pecorino. Carbonara waits for no one — the sauce is at its peak for about ninety seconds.

notes: If the eggs scramble anyway: next time pull the pan further off heat and add more pasta water first. Rescue attempt: stir in a yolk off heat; it often re-loosens the sauce.
Guanciale is widely available online and in Italian delis. Buy extra; it freezes perfectly.
The whole egg adds body, the extra yolks add silk. All-yolk versions are rounder and richer.

storage: Carbonara does not keep — the sauce breaks as it cools. If you must, refrigerate and reheat gently with a splash of water, but know that it is a different, sadder dish.

equipment.n: heavy - cast iron or stainless, for rendering the guanciale
pecorino, grated fine enough to melt instantly
coarse crack - pre-ground pepper is a different dish

facts.first_recorded: c. 1950 — startlingly young for something this canonized
facts.name_means: Most likely from carbonaro, 'charcoal worker' — though Rome argues about it daily.
facts.technique: Off-heat emulsion: eggs, cheese, pasta water, nerve
facts.signature: Guanciale fat, sheep's-milk salt, black pepper warmth
facts.serve_at: Immediately — the sauce peaks for about 90 seconds
facts.pour: Frascati, or any Roman white you would drink chilled

relations.cluster_note: Roman pasta logic: no sauce, just emulsion. Fat, starch, water, nerve.

similar.n: cheese-and-starch comfort, two nations, two temperatures
